summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's penal code criminalises homosexual conduct and carries a maximum sentence of seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained at independence and carried into its first post-independence penal code, adopted in 2015, with an enhanced sentence. OutRight Action International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, and the 2023 US State Department country report both record the prohibition as in force.

The prohibition is applied to foreign nationals as well as residents. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, an Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government described him as a dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country, and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local law including the penal code's prohibition (cited in that account as Article 600). In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one of them described as openly homosexual. Eritrea's ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the provisions of law prohibiting homosexual relations; diplomats from the teacher's country condemned the action.

Detention facilities are used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, known for housing political prisoners and journalists. The same account reports abuse, torture and beating of prisoners and some illegal executions, without giving a figure or period, and records that the UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported the death penalty was not used in 2013. The most recent documented enforcement action in this record is dated 2013; no later incident is documented.

Eritrea restricts freedom of expression and censors LGBTQ issues. A 2023 US State Department report found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by social stigma, and in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programmes detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality. The 2011 US State Department report records that the government labelled disloyal individuals gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles.

Criminalisation obstructs health care. ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing it makes prevention programmes directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern. There is no law banning conversion therapy; OutRight Action International records conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity in Eritrea, attributing them to social stigma, and LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

There is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex couples have no legal recognition and cannot adopt. The government rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appeal to legalise same-sex sexual activity as in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people, and no major effort to change or rescind the law is recorded. In 2010 Eritrea, with several other African states, rejected the Yogyakarta Principles. The UK Foreign Office report Eritrea: Country of Concern states that same-sex activity is a crime and that no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, and records that the UK raised these concerns bilaterally and through the EU.
tangentialFactors:
The 2010 US State Department Human Rights Report for Eritrea records torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service alongside the criminalisation of same-sex conduct. These conditions apply to residents and visitors generally rather than to trans travellers specifically, but they shape the detention environment into which a person suspected of same-sex conduct would be held.

The 2023 US State Department report notes that Eritrea's assault law makes no gender distinction, so an assault complaint is not framed around the sex of the parties involved.

The evidence base is uneven in date. Criminalisation is confirmed by reporting current to 2023 and to March 2026, while every documented enforcement, expulsion and detention incident in this record falls between 2003 and 2013. No incident later than 2013 is recorded, and no source supplies an enforcement rate, a charge count or a prisoner population.

The prohibition's lineage from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code is a point of comparison with other states that inherited that code; Eritrea's distinguishing feature in this record is the enhanced sentence carried into the 2015 penal code and the documented use of the provision against foreign nationals.
localsOnly:
Openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and therefore did not participate in the political process, according to the 2023 US State Department country report. The same report records continuing societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons, a finding echoed in the 2010 and 2011 reports, which record societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians.

The government's use of the label gay as an accusation against disloyal individuals, recorded in the 2011 report alongside traitors, rapists and pedophiles, indicates that the term functions officially as a charge of disloyalty rather than only as a description of conduct.

Gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have suffered physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers. This rests on a single 2002 UK refugee claimant account and is unconfirmed in the sources available here.

No public LGBTQ organisations exist, and LGBTQ people cannot assemble, associate or express themselves publicly without exposure to identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. Social stigma is recorded as the driver of conversion-therapy practices, including offers of conversion therapy in place of prosecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, entry or visa screening, bathroom and facilities access, or trans-specific health care in Eritrea. Whether Article 310(1) has been charged against a transgender person specifically is not sourced, and the record does not state how the provision is applied where the person's gender presentation does not match the sex recorded on their documents.

No trans-specific violence or killing figure appears in this inventory, and none is supplied with a denominator or a period against which it could be read. The documented incidents here are individual cases from 2003, 2004 and 2013, so the frequency of current enforcement is unresolved.

The conversion-therapy finding carries no figure and no measurement period, and the claim that prisoners are abused, tortured and beaten likewise has no count or date range attached. The military abuse account rests on one unconfirmed 2002 claimant statement.

The status of the death penalty is sourced only as of 2013, through a UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office report. Several narrative details, including the Adi Abeyto transfer and the account of the 2013 expulsion, derive from a tertiary reference compilation whose underlying citations were not verified here; no youth-specific care findings are recorded.
